This is game 19 in a series of 9×9 Go games. Each new game starts in a fresh session.

## Your goal

To become as strong at Go as you can: to keep improving, game after game, toward grandmaster-level play. The concrete target is to win consistently against the strongest opponent on the ladder, the 9d profile.

## What carries over

This session starts with no memory of the earlier ones: your conversation is not carried over. Your working directory does carry over: every file in it stays as you leave it. If AGENTS.md exists there, it is loaded into your context at the start of every session (its first 64 KiB); your other files are there to read with the file tools. What a later session knows of your earlier games is what you have left in these files.

## This game

A new game. You play Black, so you move first.

Rules: Chinese area scoring, with 7 points of komi for White; a level score is a draw. Simple ko: an immediate recapture is refused, and the board marks the ko point when there is one. Suicide is not allowed. An invalid move is refused with the rule it broke, and the turn stays with you. The game ends after two passes in a row or a resignation; a game that reaches 243 moves is scored where it stands. After two passes the engine scores the position as it stands and decides itself which stones are dead.

## Opponents

Your opponent is KataGo playing in the style of a human of the rank you choose. The ladder, weakest to strongest: 20k, 18k, 16k, 14k, 12k, 10k, 8k, 6k, 4k, 2k, 1d, 3d, 5d, 7d, 9d. You choose the rank with `choose_opponent(rank)` before the first move; it holds for the whole game, and you choose again in the next game.

## Tools

- Go: `choose_opponent(rank)`, `board()`, `play(move)` with a point or `pass`, and `resign()`.
- Files: `read_file(path)` and `list_files(path)` to read, and `apply_patch` to create, change and delete any file in your working directory.

You may write and run code. Use it only to inspect the current position and keep records — for example, to count stones or liberties, or check whether a move is legal. Do not build or use a Go engine, run Monte Carlo, search over sequences of future moves, or write a program that chooses, ranks or recommends moves.

## How this session ends

Play until the game is over. The final result comes back from your last Go call, followed by a closing note. Before you end the session after a game, write down in your working directory whatever will help the next session play better. The session ends when you end your turn.
I’ll read the previous game records, then play game 19 against 20k. I’ll check liberties and eye boundaries alongside the area count, and save the SGF and lessons after the result.

# Game 2 — White versus 12k

Result: Black wins by resignation after B45 J9. White captured one stone; Black captured none before resignation. The 17-stone upper White group was in atari at C8 and could not save itself. Exact record: game-002.sgf (45 board moves; resignation is in RE[B+R]). Chinese area, komi 7, simple ko, no suicide. No engine analysis or sequence-search program was used. Current-position liberty counting was used before every White move.

Progress: the final atari was correctly recognized, unlike game 1. However, counting liberties did not prevent a larger strategic group-safety failure. No demonstrated winning strength at 12k and still no completed scored game.

Opening and shape: White took C3/C6 and expanded through D7/D6/E7/E8. Black's B5–E5 chain separated White's upper and lower groups, while F7/F8 and then F6 restricted the upper group on the right. White's B7/B8/B6 responses to A7/A8/A6 connected the upper stones, but Black A5 joined its edge invasion to the central chain. The invasion was not captured. White's upper group had six liberties after W22 B6, but little enclosed space and no demonstrated two-eye life.

Critical contraction: after W24 E6 B25 F6, the upper group had {B9,C7,C8,D8,E9}. B29 B9 removed B9. W30 C9 created a separate two-liberty group; W32 D9 expanded that group, but B33 C8 invaded the remaining interior. Before W34 D8, the main upper group had {C7,D8,E9}, the C9–D9 pair had {D8,E9}, and Black C8 had {C7,D8}. W34 D8 joined the White groups but left only {C7,E9}; Black C8 was in atari at C7. This was a connection with two liberties and no established eyes, not safety.

White then ran along the first line: W36 E9, W38 F9, W40 G9, W42 H9. Black replied E2, G8, H8, J8. Each White extension still left the large group with just two liberties: C7 and the next point along row 9. This did not produce an escape or eye space. W44 C7 captured Black C8, leaving {C8,J9}. B45 J9 left all 17 stones with {C8}. C8 had four White neighbors, and playing there would fill the group's last liberty without capturing any Black group: suicide. Black could capture the entire group there. Resignation was based on this checked position, not a claim that the lower group was also dead.

Lessons for game 3:

- Count distinct liberties, then separately check where two eyes or an actual exit can come from. A group with several liberties can already have inadequate living space.
- Before filling an interior liberty to connect, check the merged group's liberties AND remaining eye space. W34 D8 was the clearest warning: two liberties, no established eyes, surrounded externally.
- Do not assume an enemy stone in atari means the surrounding group is safe. Capturing C8 at C7 yielded only one eye point; it could not save the group after the edge was sealed.
- Repeated first-line extensions that keep the same two-liberty count are a danger signal. The F9–H9 chase repeated game 1's edge-trapping error on a larger scale.
- Address shrinking living space earlier. This record does not establish an optimal replacement move; revisit the position before B29 B9 and before filling D8 rather than inventing a proven rescue after the enclosure.

Next training recommendation: 20k or 18k, White or Black as the user specifies, with the aim of preserving eye space and finishing a scored game. Increase rank only on demonstrated results. Keep the ultimate target of consistent wins against 9d.

# Game 1 — Black versus 9d

Result: White wins by resignation after White 40 J4. Captures: Black 0, White 6. Exact record: game-001.sgf. No external engine analysis was used; conclusions below are manual and do not establish optimal alternatives.

Opening: B E5, W C4; B F3, W D6; B F6, W E8. Black intended to develop the right and center, while White took the left/top. B7 F8 attached on the second line without checking how the stone would escape. W8 F7 and later W16 G8 left it isolated. B17 F9 and B19 G9 expanded the trapped first-line chain. It remained in atari at the end, with H9 its sole liberty. Better future practice: assess liberties and connection routes before an edge attachment; do not repeatedly invest in a chain without a viable exit.

Black invaded C7 at move 25 and followed B7/C8. The corner had room, but its life was not established. Do not record this invasion as confirmed alive or successful.

Decisive fight: W30 G6 cut between Black F6 and G7. B31 H6, W32 G5; B33 G4, W34 H5. At this point the four-stone Black chain G7-H7-J7-H6 had only J6 as a liberty. B35 J5 did not remove its atari. White instead played G2. B37 J6 joined that chain to J5, but the resulting six-stone group had only J4 as a liberty. White played F2. Black wrongly believed the connection was safe and played B39 H4; W40 J4 captured all six stones.

The exact distinct-liberty sets matter: before B39 H4, the six-stone upper-right group had {J4}, while White's G6-G5-H5 group had {F5,H4}. B39 H4 put the White group in atari at F5, but left Black's larger group in atari at J4. White captured first, opening several liberties for its own stones. This was not a successful attack.

Primary lesson: a connection can preserve atari. Count the merged group's external liberties, excluding occupied connecting points and counting shared empty points only once. Attacking a neighboring group does not protect your own group if the opponent can capture it immediately.

Training for game 2: use explicit liberty counts every turn; fix endangered groups before new invasions; play against an easier profile if useful to practice complete games and area scoring. Avoid claiming a move is best from this single unreviewed loss. Record recurring errors and results so progress can be measured.

# Game 3 — Black versus 20k

Result: White wins by 16 points (W+16), after B45 pass and W46 pass. First completed scored game in the series; no win demonstrated at 20k. Chinese area, komi 7, simple ko, no suicide. Captures before scoring: 0 for both players. Exact record: game-003.sgf. No engine analysis, move-ranking code, or sequence-search program was used. Existing-group distinct liberties were inspected after every opponent reply; strategic judgments below are manual, not established optimal play.

Opening: B E5/G3/G7, followed by G2/G4/F4/F5. White took C7 and built along D4–D6, with F1–F3 below. Black extended E6/E7/D7/D8/D9 while White connected C6/C8/C9. This built a connected Black boundary but also let White develop much of the left side. B25 F7 joined G7 to the main chain. W26 H2 entered the lower right; B27 H3 and B29 J3 blocked upward expansion, but W30 H1 connected the invasion to the bottom White stones. The right-side space alone did not win with komi. Future practice: assess the territorial balance while developing; repeatedly answering local boundary moves can leave too little elsewhere. This record does not prove an optimal opening replacement.

Failed invasion: B31 C3 had four liberties {B3,C2,C4,D3}, but no eyes. W32 D2 restricted the bottom. B33 C4 extended toward White D4; W34 C2 removed the lower liberty. B35 C5 extended toward White C6/D5. W36 B3 left the three-stone chain with {B4,B5,D3}. It had no established eye space and no clear exit. Recognizing danger only here was too late to establish a rescue in this game.

B37 B5, W38 B6 left {A5,B4,D3}. B39 B4 joined internally but still left only {A4,A5,D3}; it did not improve the liberty count or establish eyes. W40 B2 joined White B3 to C2/D2, removing the prospect of capturing an isolated B3 stone easily. B41 A5 left {A4,A6,D3}. W42 D3 joined White's upper and lower chains, leaving Black only {A4,A6}. B43 A6 filled one liberty and gained A7; W44 A7 left seven Black stones {A5,A6,B4,B5,C3,C4,C5} in atari at A4. A4 would leave only A3, still without eyes or an exit. Black passed, and White passed; the scorer returned W+16 with those stones still on the board. No explicit dead-stone breakdown was returned.

The main right-side chain had ten distinct liberties at the end: {E8,E9,F6,F8,G5,G6,G8,H4,H7,J4}. Its safety was not the decisive failure. The seven-stone invasion was recognized as lost before passing; unlike game 1, its atari was not overlooked.

Lessons for game 4:

- Liberty counting worked as observation, but did not prevent enclosure. A four-liberty invasion can have poor prospects if extensions lead toward enemy strength and there is no plan for two eyes or an exit.
- Before invading, identify usable living space and how the opponent can block access to it. C3's open-looking corner was restricted immediately by D2/C2 and then B3.
- Reassess after each restricting reply. By W34 C2, Black had four liberties but only leftward space; B35 C5 added stones toward the strong upper White chain rather than widening living space.
- Do not equate connecting or maintaining three liberties with progress. B39 B4 left the same count and reduced interior room; A5/A6 repeated the earlier games' edge-running pattern.
- Avoid investing more stones in an enclosure just to prolong atari. A rescue needs a concrete capture, eye-space improvement, or exit.
- Keep a rough area balance in mind before the board is partitioned. Securing one side can still be insufficient with White's komi and lower-right gains.
- Passing was appropriate only after checking that the endangered group had no identified rescue and the remaining boundary had no identified profitable move. This manual assessment is not an engine-certified claim.

Next training recommendation: stay at 20k. Aim to establish eye space before enclosure and finish another scored game, seeking an actual win before increasing rank. Ultimate target remains consistent wins against 9d.

# Game 4 — White versus 20k

Result: Black wins by 10 points (B+10), after W58 pass and B59 pass. Chinese area, komi 7, simple ko, no suicide. Captures before scoring: White 1, Black 0. Exact record: game-004.sgf. Second scored game; still no demonstrated win at 20k. Current-position group/liberty inspection was used after every opponent board move. No engine analysis, move-ranking program, or future-sequence search was used. Strategic conclusions are manual and do not establish optimal alternatives.

Lower-left opening: W2 C3, B3 D3; W4 C4, B5 C5; W6 D4, B7 D5; W8 E4, B9 F4. White pushed below Black's wall. W10 E3 put D3 in atari; B11 E2 did not save it. W12 D2 captured D3. W14 C2 joined D2 through the outside, preserving D3 as an eye rather than filling it to connect. W16 B3 and W18 A3 closed the left boundary. W20 C7 changed areas; B21 D1 invaded the bottom boundary, answered by W22 C1 and B23 E1. The final lower-left chain had {A2,B1,B2,D3}, plus corner space A1. D3 was an enclosed eye and the lower-left corner provided additional eye space. This was better eye preservation than game 2.

Upper development: W20 C7, W24 D7, W26 E7, W28 E8. After B29 B7, White closed the left edge with C8/C9 while Black followed B8/B9. White then extended F8/G8/H8/J8, with Black playing G7/H7/J7 beneath. Unlike the trapped first-line runs in previous games, this connected boundary retained substantial interior space. After Black filled C6/D6, the final upper group's seven liberties were {D8,D9,E9,F9,G9,H9,J9}. These empty points included a broad region behind the White boundary; White did not fill them just to connect.

Failed right-side development: W42 H3 entered the open lower right because the existing upper and lower-left areas appeared insufficient. However, the plan was only 'there is room to develop eyes', not an identified pair of usable eye regions. B43 H2 immediately took the route toward the bottom corner. W44 H4 and W46 H5 expanded upward. B47 G4 restricted the left. W48 G5, B49 F5; W50 G6, B51 F6. Black F6 joined the row-7 chain to the large central/lower chain, removing the prospect of an easy capture above. White's right group then had {G3,H6,J3,J4,J5}: five liberties, no established eyes. This was the critical reassessment point.

W52 H6 expanded toward the top edge, but B53 D6 left the surrounding Black chain with six liberties. W54 J3 and B55 G2 joined Black H2 to that chain. W56 J2, B57 H1 blocked the bottom route. The eight White stones {G5,G6,H3,H4,H5,H6,J2,J3} finished with {G3,J1,J4,J5,J6}. G3 bordered Black F3/G4/G2; J1 bordered Black H1; J6 bordered Black J7. These were liberties, not enclosed White eyes. J4/J5 were adjacent empty points, not two separate eyes. No concrete capture, two-eye construction, or exit was identified. White stopped investing and passed; Black passed. The scorer returned B+10 without a dead-stone breakdown, so the exact automatic treatment of the right group was not separately reported.

Lessons for game 5:

- Preserve the successful outside connection pattern: C2 joined the lower group while leaving the captured point D3 as an eye. Connection and eye space should be checked separately.
- Before a new isolated group, name two potential eye regions and identify the opponent's moves that could remove them. Open points near an edge are not automatically usable living space.
- Reassess immediately after a reply takes one of those regions. B43 H2 removed the bottom-corner route; B51 F6 connected the enclosing chains. Continuing merely because the group had five liberties repeated the central error of games 2 and 3.
- For each candidate eye point, check all orthogonal neighbors. A liberty bordering a strong enemy chain is not an enclosed eye. Adjacent empty points such as J4/J5 usually form one eye region, not two eyes.
- Plan area balance earlier. White's upper and lower-left holdings together were roughly 32 area points; komi brought that to 39 against approximately 49 if Black controlled the remainder. That rough count matched the final margin, but does not prove a precise dead-stone breakdown. Earlier broader development might avoid needing a late isolated group; no optimal replacement move is established here.
- Five liberties can coexist with a strategically lost enclosure. Recognize that before atari and avoid adding stones solely to prolong it.

Next training recommendation: remain at 20k and seek a scored win before increasing rank. Aim to develop connected frameworks with usable eye space and count rough area before the board is partitioned. The long-term target remains consistent wins against 9d.

# Game 6 — White versus 20k

Result: Black wins by 26 points (B+26), after W56 pass and B57 pass. Chinese area, komi 7, simple ko, no suicide. Captures before scoring: White 2, Black 0. Exact record: game-006.sgf. Fourth scored game; no win yet at any rank. Current-position distinct liberties were counted after every opponent board move. No engine analysis, move-ranking code, or future-sequence search was used. Tactical and strategic conclusions below are manual.

Opening: W2 C3 and W4 C6 took the left; W6 D7, W8 D6 built upward while Black occupied E5/E3/G6/E7. W10 C4, W12 D4, W14 D5 connected the left boundary. B15 D8 capped the upper route. W16 E4 extended the boundary, but B17 F4 blocked further expansion. The connected White group had six liberties and broad left space, but too little prospective area by itself. This was recognized before entering the lower right, yet the new group's life plan remained too vague.

Lower-right failure: W18 G3 was earlier than game 4's invasion, with open bottom and corner space. However, those directions were not independently secured eye regions. W20 H3, B21 F3; W22 G2, B23 F2; W24 G1, B25 J2. White answered the invasion with W26 J3 and W28 H2; B29 J1 left Black J1/J2 in atari at H1. W30 H1 correctly captured both stones. At that point the White group, after B31 G4, had only {F1,J1,J2}. J1/J2 formed ONE eye region; the capture did not establish two-eye life. The only external route was F1. W32 F1, B33 E1 left eight White stones {F1,G1,G2,G3,H1,H2,H3,J3} with {J1,J2}, no exit and no second eye. White correctly stopped adding stones then, but recognized the enclosure too late. Playing inside the two-point region would reduce the group's liberties to one; no capture or rescue was identified.

Left boundary completion: W34 C7, W36 B7, W38 A7 were answered by C8/B8/A8. W40 C2, W42 B2, W44 A2, W46 A1 closed the bottom boundary against C1/B1/D1. The final 15-stone left chain had {A3,A6,B3,B4,B6,C5}, with a broad connected interior behind it. Preserving that space was useful, but this framework occupied only roughly 24 area points, far short of a winning share even with komi.

Second failed entry: After B47 G7, White reconsidered passing because the upper right was open. W48 H8 had three liberties after B49 G8, and W50 H7 still had three after B51 H6: {H9,J7,J8}. Those were already a narrow corridor, not two secured eye regions. W52 J7, B53 J6 left {H9,J8}; W54 H9, B55 G9 left four stones {H7,H8,H9,J7} with {J8,J9}. Again these were one adjacent two-point eye region with no exit. The proposed top/right living areas overlapped and Black sealed their boundaries in successive replies. White passed rather than fill the remaining region; Black passed.

The scorer returned B+26 without a dead-stone breakdown. A rough partition of 24 White area versus 57 Black area gives the same margin with komi 7, but this is a consistency check, not an explicit report of how each group was adjudicated.

Lessons for game 7:

- Naming two directions is insufficient. Name two DISTINCT potential eye regions and the boundary points required to preserve each. Bottom and corner space in the lower right collapsed into the same J1/J2 region.
- A capture can be tactically correct while the group remains strategically enclosed. After W30 H1, explicitly count eyes separately from liberties: three liberties, one eye region, and only F1 as an external route.
- Check closure threats before answering an interior invasion. J2 diverted moves while Black F2/F3/G4 and later E1 sealed the outside. This record does not prove an optimal alternative, but the assessment must happen before the enclosure is complete.
- Reassess a new group after its FIRST restrictive reply. After B49 G8 and especially B51 H6, the upper-right group's three liberties did not imply adequate living space. H7/J7 extended a narrow boundary without securing eyes.
- Do not repeat a failed corner pattern elsewhere in the same game. Both right groups finished with exactly one two-point eye region.
- Maintain the successful connected boundary and open interior, but contest a larger share earlier. By B15 D8, the left framework was capped; continuing local development could not supply enough area.
- Liberty counting is now exposing failures accurately, but must change decisions earlier. Another completed loss is not evidence of improved playing strength.

Next training recommendation: remain at 20k. Aim for an actual scored win through early area balance and groups with distinct usable eye space or checked outside connections. Ultimate target remains consistent wins against 9d.

# Game 5 — Black versus 20k

Result: White wins by 8 points (W+8), after B39 pass and W40 pass. Chinese area, komi 7, simple ko, no suicide. Captures before scoring: 0 for both players. Exact record: game-005.sgf. Third scored game; still no demonstrated win at 20k. Existing-group distinct liberties were inspected after each opponent board move. No engine analysis, move-ranking code, or future-sequence search was used. Strategic and tactical judgments were manual and are not certified optimal.

Opening: B E5/E4/E6/F6 formed a connected central boundary while White occupied D5/D6/E7/F7. B9 D4 and B11 C3 expanded toward the lower left; B13 D3 connected C3 to the main chain. B15 B3, W16 A3; B17 A2 left the new stone with {A1,B2}. B19 B2 connected outside, giving the merged group eight liberties and leaving the bottom space open. This connection was checked, unlike game 1's fatal connection. There were no established separate eyes yet, but substantial open space below the boundary.

Right boundary: B21 G6, W22 H6; B23 H5, W24 J6; B25 J5, W26 H8. The H5/J5 pair retained {G5,H4,J4}. B27 G5 joined it to the main chain, producing ten liberties after W28 H7: {A1,B1,C2,D2,E3,F4,F5,G4,H4,J4}. White H7 joined its upper and right stones. Black retained broad lower-board space but only about 40 prospective area points against about 41 for White before komi. This was a rough framework count, not a secure territory count or a dead-stone calculation. It already suggested a deficit of about eight.

Failed cut: Before B29 C5, White's separate left chain {A3,A4,B4,C4} had {A5,B5,C5}. Black tried to exploit these three liberties. C5 itself had only {B5,C6}, no eye, and no connection to the main chain. The tactical expectation was flawed: W30 B5 filled B5 but ADDED B6 as a liberty, leaving White {A5,B6}, while Black C5 was in atari at C6. Black had initially expected only A5. Always count the extension's newly exposed empty neighbors, not just the old liberties it fills.

B31 C6, W32 B6 left the two Black stones with sole liberty C7. White's left chain now had {A5,A6,B7}; its extension again added liberties. B33 C7, W34 B7 left sole liberty C8. B35 C8 gained access to the upper-left space, but W36 D8 restricted the chain to {B8,C9}. B37 B8, W38 A8 left five Black stones {B8,C5,C6,C7,C8} with {B9,C9}. There were no established eyes. White A8 had {A7,A9}, the left White chain had {A5,A6,A7}, and the large upper White chain had seven liberties. The hoped-for upper-left space was closed without establishing life or a concrete capture.

Black stopped investing and passed; White passed. The scorer returned W+8 with all stones still shown and no explicit dead-stone breakdown. Do not infer the exact treatment of the cutting group from that margin. No rescue was identified manually; that is not a proof that every continuation fails or that passing was optimal.

Lessons for game 6:

- When attacking a low-liberty enemy chain, account for NEW liberties created by its extension. The B5/B6 replies invalidated the intended capture; filling one old liberty does not necessarily reduce the count.
- A cut needs a concrete capture, connection, or two-eye plan. C5 began with two liberties and no established eyes; calling the upper-left corner open was insufficient.
- Recognize a forced-running pattern early. C6/C7 were successive atari responses; C8 briefly gained space, but D8 removed the right route. Reassess before adding B8, not only after A8 seals the enclosure.
- Keep the useful outside connections: D3, B2, and G5 joined groups with checked merged liberties while retaining lower interior space.
- Assess area sooner. The connected lower boundary was too small with komi once White secured the top and left. A late risky cut did not solve that strategic deficit.
- A smaller losing margin is not evidence of winning strength. Remain at 20k until actual results justify moving up. The long-term goal remains consistent wins against 9d.

# Game 11 — Black versus 20k

Result: White wins by 32 points (W+32), after B43 pass and W44 pass. Chinese area, komi 7, simple ko, no suicide. Captures before scoring: none. Exact record: game-011.sgf. Series: nine scored games, nine losses, one win, one draw. Consistent winning strength is not demonstrated.

All ten prior records were read. Current-position code listed groups and distinct liberties after each opponent reply from W4 onward; B1 was checked manually. Candidate effects were assessed manually. Empty connected regions were counted before passing. No engine, Monte Carlo, future-sequence search, or move-ranking program was used. Conclusions do not establish optimal alternatives.

Opening: B E5/C7/G7, W C3/G3/E3. Black had three opening stones pointing toward the top, but did not secure a sufficiently large share. B7 E4 attached above E3; D5/D6 and F5/F6 formed the central boundary while White D4/F4 occupied beneath it. B17 C6 connected C7 to the main chain; B23 G6 joined G7 through F6. These connections retained five and seven liberties respectively after the replies. They prevented isolated opening-group losses, but the central boundary left most of the bottom to White.

Edge development: C8/C9 answered B7/B8 and closed the top-left boundary. G8/G9/H9/J9 closed the upper right while White H6/H7/H8/J8 occupied outside. B33 B9 and B41 A9 claimed shared top-left points while remaining connected. This first-line play was attached to the main framework with substantial interior room, unlike the trapped isolated runs in games 1–3. It still gained too little area. By W26 H8, the narrow top framework and White's occupation below already indicated a large deficit; the exact count came only at the end.

Failed bottom entry: B35 E2 had a proposed left region around C1/D1 and a right region around F1/G1, but neither had secured boundaries. Required points included C2/D2 and F2/G2. W36 F2 immediately occupied one required boundary and left E2 with {D2,E1}. B37 D2 expanded left; W38 D3 joined White C3/D4/E3 and left Black {C2,D1,E1}. B39 C2 continued toward the corner, but W40 B2 removed that route. The three Black stones {C2,D2,E2} finished with {C1,D1,E1}. Those adjacent points form one connected first-line strip. B1 and F1 were still open enemy entry routes at its ends, so it was not three private eyes. No concrete capture, second eye, or exit was identified. Black stopped investing and completed A9, then passed. This is not an exhaustive proof that every rescue fails.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"// Current-position inspection only. No move generation or future search.
// Paste this function into functions.exec and call it with the text returned
// by board()/play(). Its result lists existing chains and distinct liberties.
function inspectLiberties(boardText) {
  const columns = 'ABCDEFGHJ';
  const cells = new Map();
  for (const line of boardText.split('\n')) {
    const m = line.match(/^\s*([1-9])\s+([XO.](?:\s+[XO.]){8})\s+[1-9]\s*$/);
    if (m) m[2].split(/\s+/).forEach((v, x) => cells.set(columns[x] + m[1], v));
  }
  if (cells.size !== 81) throw new Error('Expected a complete 9x9 text board');
  function neighbors(p) {
    const x = columns.indexOf(p[0]), y = Number(p[1]);
    return [[x-1,y],[x+1,y],[x,y-1],[x,y+1]]
      .filter(([a,b]) => a >= 0 && a < 9 && b >= 1 && b <= 9)
      .map(([a,b]) => columns[a]+b);
  }
  const seen = new Set(), groups = [];
  for (const [point, color] of cells) {
    if (color === '.' || seen.has(point)) continue;
    const stones = [], liberties = new Set(), stack = [point];
    seen.add(point);
    while (stack.length) {
      const p = stack.pop(); stones.push(p);
      for (const q of neighbors(p)) {
        if (cells.get(q) === '.') liberties.add(q);
        else if (cells.get(q) === color && !seen.has(q)) {
          seen.add(q); stack.push(q);
        }
      }
    }
    groups.push({ color, stones: stones.sort(), liberties: [...liberties].sort(), count: liberties.size });
  }
  return groups;
}

W28 J7 and W34 J8 closed the right exit. No concrete rescue was identified; this is not an exhaustive proof that every earlier alternative fails. B29 H4 joined the lower-right Black chains, preserving six liberties before the reply. W36 F9 left the upper ten stones in atari at J9. Black J9 would have been suicide: it would fill the last liberty without capturing the large White chain, which had ten liberties. Black did not spend another stone there; W38 J9 captured all ten. Accurate recognition of the final atari did not repair the earlier strategic failure.

Lower framework: F3/F2/E2/D2 expanded through existing connections into the open bottom, followed by D3/C2/C1. White C3/B2 restricted the left, but this group retained substantial bottom space. J6 closed the right boundary against J7; E3 filled the last shared point. No unsupported late invasion was added. The final Black chain had fourteen stones and seven liberties {D1,E1,F1,G2,H3,J4,J5}. Its thirteen-point empty region was {D1,E1,F1,G1,G2,H1,H2,H3,J1,J2,J3,J4,J5}, bordered only by Black. It was one connected region with room to separate eyes: F1 could divide the two-point D1/E1 strip from the right-side region. No exhaustive life proof was performed; scoring retained Black's counted area.

Final exact current-board count: Black 14 stones + 13 empties = 27. White 23 stones + 21 left-side empties + ten emptied capture points = 54, plus komi 7 = 61. No mixed-border empty region remained. 61 - 27 = 34, matching W+34. The scorer returned no separate dead-stone breakdown.

Lessons for game 16:

- When an opponent occupies the connection route between original footholds, reassess immediately. F5/G5/G6 separated the upper and lower groups; continuing F7/G8/F8 did not recover useful eye space. Review the position before B11 F6 and B13 H5, rather than assuming a particular replacement works.
- A framework count must use disjoint point sets. Count stones separately from EMPTY conditional regions; subtract enemy stones and already counted friendly stones. This game's announced 48 was actually 46 even under optimistic ownership assumptions.
- Recompute the allocation when a required boundary is lost. G7 and D7 invalidated the proposed 46-point framework, but play continued along the same shrinking boundary.
- Audit original-group eye space before extending another edge stone. After D7/D8, the upper group had two liberties and no eyes. G8/F8 merged stones but did not create a second eye or a durable exit.
- Do not describe a sequence of top-line connections as a rescue without naming its resulting eye regions. At B27 G9, F9 touched White E9 and J9 bordered White's corner access; two liberties were not two eyes.
- Recognizing an unsavable last liberty can avoid wasting a stone, but the improvement needed is earlier preservation of living space. W36 F9 was already far too late to repair this enclosure.
- Preserve connected expansion into open bottom space and exact region counting, but 27 surviving area cannot win. A large original-group loss remains the decisive failure.
- Stay at 20k. One win, one draw, thirteen losses do not support promotion. Keep the target of consistent wins against human-style 9d.

Tools and analysis code may inspect the current board, count liberties and check legality; never build/use an engine, Monte Carlo, future-sequence search, or a program recommending/ranking moves.

Critical improvement: count DISTINCT liberties of ALL endangered friendly groups before each move. Joining groups does not guarantee safety. Check again after selecting a move, especially if it fills a friendly liberty. Game 1 lost six connected stones because the sole liberty J4 was overlooked. Use current-position-liberties.js as a counting aid, not as a move selector.

Before tenuki, identify opponent's immediate captures and cuts. Treat groups with one liberty as emergencies and two liberties as tactical concerns. Near the first line, assess escape routes before attaching: F8 in game 1 became trapped after F7/G8, and chasing along row 9 did not create an escape.

Do not describe groups as alive, connected safely, or enemy stones as dead without checking actual liberties and eye space. Distinguish observations from unverified strategic impressions.

Game 2 improvement: liberty counting alone is insufficient. Check actual eye space and an exit before enclosure. W34 D8 joined the upper group but left two liberties and no established eyes. Running F9/G9/H9 kept two liberties without escaping. Capturing C8 with C7 created only one eye; B45 J9 left 17 White stones with sole liberty C8, which White could not fill legally. But W42 H3 entered the lower right without naming two usable eye regions. B43 H2 blocked the bottom route; B51 F6 joined the enclosing Black chains.
